newsitem.title: USA: Black workers accuse UPS of race discrimination.
newsitem.headline: Black workers accuse UPS of race discrimination.

text.p: Sixteen black employees of United Parcel Service of America Inc. filed a class-action lawsuit against the package delivery giant on Wednesday, accusing it of racial discrimination.

The lawsuit was filed in federal court in Oakland on behalf of all African-American hourly employees and part-time supervisors at UPS in Alaska, Arizona, California, Hawaii, Idaho, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah and Washington.

The suit alleges that UPS has a policy of denying desirable job assignments, training and promotional opportunities to black employees. It accuses UPS of discriminating against its black employees in working conditions, pay and other terms of employment.

Some of the black UPS workers who filed suit alleged they were passed over for promotion in favor of less experienced workers of other races and that they were assigned to drive routes in more dangerous areas than other drivers. Several said they had been subjected to a racially-hostile work environment.

"We hope that a lot of changes can be made at UPS promotional-wise, (and that) the African-American will be able to move up in the company -- top levels, not the bottom levels," one of the plaintiffs, Maran Wilson, told Reuters.

The lawsuit said that Wilson, 49, an Oakland-based package car driver who has worked for UPS for 22 years, had been denied job assignments and promotional opportunities offered to "similarly situated non-African Americans."

The Oakland branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), which conducted a year-long investigation of the allegations by UPS employees, estimated that there were several thousand class members who potentially could be covered by the suit.

"Today, we demonstrate our belief that the courts will ensure equal opportunities for all workers, irrespective of their race," Shannon Reeves, president of the Oakland branch of the NAACP, said in a statement.
Responding to the lawsuit, UPS said it "does not tolerate discrimination of any kind."

It said it took the concerns of its employees very seriously, but regretted that its efforts to engage in a meaningful dialogue with all the interested parties involved in the suit "have not been met with a positive response."

"We will continue to investigate these claims in the hope of ensuring every UPS employee continues to work in an environment free of discrimination, harassment or mistreatment of any kind," the UPS statement said.

The lawsuit said that Erskine Garrette, a UPS driver in San Diego, had been assigned to routes in more dangerous areas than less senior drivers who were not black. Routes in more desirable, predominantly white, neighborhoods had been given to less senior, white drivers who were purported to have "more familiarity" with the routes, it said.
UPS spokesman Tom Pizzuti said most routes were posted and awarded to the most senior driver who bid for them.

The lawsuit seeks a court order barring UPS from engaging in the alleged unlawful practices and an order that UPS must institute policies that provide equal employment opportunities for African Americans.

It also seeks an order "restoring class members to their rightful positions at UPS" and adjustments in wage rates, benefits and seniority rights for class members to the level they "would be enjoying but for UPS's discriminatory practices."

The lawsuit also seeks unspecified damages for alleged lost compensation, job benefits and emotional distress as well as punitive damages" in an amount commensurate with UPS's ability to pay and to deter future conduct."
UPS employs about 339,000 people worldwide and offers package delivery service in about 200 countries.
